---
title: "What this project cannot tell you"
subtitle: "Limitations, stated plainly"
---

Good analysis is clear about its own limits. This page collects the ceilings that
apply to the maps on this site, in one place, so they are not buried in captions or
lost between pages. None of them is a reason to distrust the work — each is a reason
to read a specific result at its true strength, no more.

The limitations fall into two kinds: what the **corridor** can and cannot claim, and
what the **descriptive maps** (density, hot spots) can and cannot claim. A short note
on the data inputs follows.

## The corridor is a hypothesis, not a tracked path

The puma corridor is the single result most likely to be over-read, so it gets the
plainest statement.

- **No animal was tracked.** The corridor is built entirely from the landscape —
  land cover, human modification, slope, and traffic. This project has **no GPS-collar
  or telemetry data** of its own. So the corridor is a *modelled hypothesis* about
  where movement is cheapest, not a record of where pumas actually went. Strong
  validation would need collar data showing animals using the route; this project
  cannot provide that, and does not claim it.
- **The route is weighted by author-set priors.** The resistance surface blends its
  inputs on weights chosen by the analyst (45% human modification, 40% land cover,
  15% slope), with directions and the traffic transform taken from published
  Santa Cruz Mountains puma work. The weights are sourced and reasonable, but they
  are priors, not fitted values — this project has no local movement data to fit them
  against.

### How much the route can move: about 1.5 km of play

The corridor's **location is stable**; its **exact centre-line is not.** When the
gHM/land-cover weight was perturbed by ±10% (a pre-registered sensitivity test), the
broad corridor barely changed — the worst-case overlap of the wide context band
stayed very high (IoU 0.941). But the single least-cost line shifted, and under
gHM-heavy weighting the path shortened from 37.2 km to 35.6 km, a route play of
**about 1.5 km**. This is exactly why the corridor is published as a two-tier
**swath**, not a line: the band is honest about the play, the line is not.

::: {.callout-note title="Read the band, not the line"}
A 1 km analysis grain is also coarser than the features it crosses. At the Coyote
Valley pinch, the least-cost line passes about 1.6 km from the exact pinch cell —
not an error, just the grain. The swath locates the corridor regionally; the
road-crossing step, not the centre-line, locates the pinch.
:::

### The core-connectivity network has a cross-bay artifact

A second connectivity product — the network graph linking large habitat cores —
carries a specific, named artifact that must not be over-read.

- The network is built with a **Gabriel graph**, which connects cores that are
  geometric neighbours. Across the central Bay, that forces edges **over the water**,
  which is an impassable barrier for a puma. So the longest cross-bay links in the
  network are **not candidate corridors** — they are evidence that those clusters are
  *disconnected*, which is the opposite of a route to protect.
- What survives this caveat: the **ranking** of links by cost is valid within the
  graph, the **two-subnetwork finding** (the central Bay splits a Peninsula /
  Santa Cruz Mountains subnetwork from an East Bay / Diablo one, joined efficiently
  only at the south) is real and matches known Santa Cruz Mountains puma isolation,
  and the contrast between cheap south-Bay links and costly cross-bay links holds.
  What does **not** survive: reading any individual cross-bay link as a protectable
  corridor. The site's network map shows the cost-ranked edges and flags the cross-bay
  links with this caveat; it does not draw a labelled route across the bay.

::: {.callout-note title="A correction on the record"}
An earlier version of this network stated a specific node count and a specific
core-to-core chain. Both were wrong — the stated cutoff disagreed with the code as
run, and the chain was never actually traced. The error was found, documented, and
corrected, with the original text preserved for audit. The ranking and the
two-subnetwork finding were unaffected and still stand. The correction is recorded
in the methodology log (Decisions 37–38).
:::

## The descriptive maps are shaped by where people looked

The density (KDE) and hot-spot (Gi\*) maps describe **records**, and records are made
by people, unevenly. This is the effort problem, and it is the subject of its own
page — but it belongs in any honest list of limits.

- **Every descriptive surface is effort-shaped.** A warm density zone or a red hot
  spot can mean "many animals" or "many observers." The two tracks handle this
  differently — the bobcat occupancy model removes the effort signal, so it
  *diverges* from the raw density; the puma corridor never contains an effort signal,
  so its *convergence* with the raw density is informative rather than circular — but
  no descriptive map escapes it.
- **The puma hot-spot map is about half effort.** Of the puma record hot-spots, only
  a minority survive the effort cross-check as trusted; the rest coincide with survey
  effort and are flagged suspect on the map. A red unit is not proof of pumas until
  that check clears it.
- **The convergence is corroboration, not proof.** Where the corridor and the record
  density agree, part of that agreement is structural — both rest on the same
  land-cover and human-modification gradient — so it is read as weak-to-moderate
  corroboration, not validation.

## Data-input limits worth stating

These are smaller, but each shapes a specific result and each is carried openly
rather than smoothed over.

- **Chaparral is under-mapped — but it does not move the corridor.** The land-cover
  source (ESA WorldCover) badly under-maps California chaparral, prime cat habitat.
  This *sounds* serious for a habitat model. A pre-registered sensitivity test bounded
  it: rebuilding the resistance surface with chaparral treated as good habitat changed
  the corridor essentially not at all (overlap IoU 1.000 / 0.998). So the under-mapping
  is **immaterial to connectivity** — stated because it is real, not because it
  changes the result.
- **Traffic counts are biased upward off the highways.** Measured traffic covers state
  highways; local and arterial roads are filled in from the nearest measured segment
  or a class-based floor (about 19,851 segments spatially filled, and roughly 45% on a
  modelled floor). Because count stations cluster on busy roads, that fill runs
  high. The effect is compressed by the log-inverse traffic transform and bounded by a
  sensitivity check, but it is a real property of the data, tracked with a source flag
  on every segment rather than hidden.
- **The analysis grain is regional.** The puma surfaces are built at a 1 km grain,
  which is coarse for sub-kilometre features like a single road pinch. The surfaces
  are regional context; the crossing-point analysis, not the surface, resolves the
  fine detail.

## Two whole questions left open

- **Road mortality is incomplete.** The wildlife–vehicle collision question is
  currently answered as a risk-overlap proxy, because record-level roadkill data is
  still pending. The collision-risk page says so directly and is marked incomplete.
- **No population trend is possible.** There is no repeated regional census of either
  species. A one-time statewide puma estimate exists as context; no statewide bobcat
  estimate exists at all. Nothing on this site should be read as a population trend.

---

Every limitation above is recorded in full, with its sensitivity test and its
figures, in
[`docs/methodology.md`](https://github.com/K-bsub/bay-area-wildcats/blob/main/docs/methodology.md).
The point of gathering them here is the project's first principle: state the ceiling,
do not bury it.
